figures.text: Fig. 1 Schematic illustration of bacNID-mediated MurD degradation for antibacterial therapy. a Starting from UDP-GlcNAc, MurD, along with other Mur ligases, catalyzes the synthesis of peptidoglycan for bacterial cell wall formation. MurD specifically catalyzes the addition of D-glutamic acid (D-Glu) onto UDP-MurNAc-L-Ala. b ClpXP is a AAA+ protease complex that uses the energy from ATP to degrade proteins within bacteria. This protease complex consists of two main components: the hexameric AAA+ ATPase ClpX and the tetradecameric peptidase ClpP. ClpX binds to SsrA-tagged proteins, unfolds them using ATP energy, and translocates the unfolded polypeptides into ClpP’s proteolytic chamber, where they are degraded. While ClpXP can degrade SsrA-tagged proteins without SspB, the presence of SspB facilitates their efficient degradation at low substrate concentrations. The SspB adapter can bind to an SsrA tag and deliver the SsrA-tagged proteins to ClpXP for subsequent efficient degradation. c In order to degrade MurD in bacteria, bacNIDs are synthesized by modifying the MurD targeting peptide and the SsrA peptide on GNPs (ii). After entering bacteria, bacNIDs bind to MurD and recruit SspB to target ClpXP for target protein degradation (ii). Degradation of MurD prevents the formation of the bacterial cell wall, leading to fragmentation and death of S. aureus and S. typhimurium . Importantly, repeated use of bacNIDs does not lead to bacterial resistance.

Fig. 2 Preparation and characterization of bacNIDs. a Schematic representation of bacNIDs preparation, illustrating the nanoplatform connecting pMurD and tSsrA via gold-sulfur coordination and enhancing bacterial entry. b Close-up views and electrostatic surface representations of pMurD binding to the major pocket in MurD of S. typhimurium . MurD and pMurD are depicted in gray and color, respectively. A magnified view of the interaction of MurD of S. typhimurium with pMurD is shown in the dashed box. Amino acids involved in hydrogen bond formation are connected with green dashed lines. c Close-up views (left) and ribbon diagram (right) of the electrostatic surface representations of tSsrA binding to the major pocket in SspB of S. typhimurium . SspB and tSsrA are depicted in green and orange, respectively. A magnified view of the interaction of SspB of S. typhimurium with tSsrA is shown in the dashed box. d TEM image and size distribution of GNPs. Scale bar, 5 nm. e TEM image and size distribution of bacNIDs. Scale bar, 5 nm. f Confocal images of S. aureus and S. typhimurium treated with fluorochrome-labeled tSsrA or bacNIDs. Scale bar, 20 μm. Data in panels ( d – f ) are representative of two biologically independent experiments. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Fig. 3 Specific degradation of MurD and antibacterial activity of bacNIDs. a Immunoblot data showing MurD levels in S. aureus and S. typhimurium treated with bacNIDs at indicated concentrations for 12 h. b Immunoblot data showing MurD levels in S. aureus and S. typhimurium treated with GNPs, M-GNPs, S-GNPs, and bacNIDs. Relative optical density (OD600) of planktonic growth suspension of S. aureus ( c ) and S. typhimurium ( d ) after 12 h of incubation under the indicated treatments. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 biologically independent samples). e Immunoblot data showing MurD levels in bacNID-treated S. aureus without or with (3 R, 4 R)-A2-32-01 (50 μM) for 12 h. f Optical density (OD600) of planktonic growth suspension of S. aureus treated with bacNIDs and (3 R, 4 R)-A2-32-01 (50 μM) for 12 h. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 biologically independent samples). Photographs ( g ) and quantitative analysis ( h ) of colony formation of S. aureus and S. typhimurium after GNP, M-GNP, S-GNP, or bacNID treatments. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 biologically independent samples). i Inhibition zone and quantitative analysis of GNPs, M-GNPs, S-GNPs, or bacNIDs against S. aureus . Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 biologically independent samples). j Inhibition zone and quantitative analysis of GNPs, M-GNPs, S-GNPs, or bacNIDs against S. typhimurium . Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 biologically independent samples). Statistical significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test in ( h – j ). Data in panels a , b and e are representative of two biologically independent experiments. Source data are provided in the Source Data file.

Fig. 4 Antibacterial mechanism and drug resistance evaluation. a SEM image of S. aureus and S. typhimurium ( b ) after PBS, GNP, M-GNP, S-GNP, or bacNID treatments. Scale bar, 5 µm for bottom image; 1 µm for top image. c Live/dead staining of S. aureus and S. typhimurium ( d ) with indicated treatments. Scale bar, 20 µm. e Measurements of DNA and ATP in the supernatants of S. aureus after indicated treatments. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 biologically independent samples). f Measurements of DNA and ATP in the supernatants of S. typhimurium after indicated treatments. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 biologically independent samples). g Antimicrobial resistance testing of bacNIDs and norfloxacin against S. aureus and S. typhimurium . h OD600 of planktonic growth suspension of drug-resistant S. aureus-5 and S. typhimurium-8 treated with bacNIDs. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 biologically independent samples). i Photographs of colony formation of S. aureus-5 and S. typhimurium-8 after PBS, norfloxacin ( S. aureus- 5: 10 μM, S. typhimurium -8: 200 nM), and bacNIDs ( S. aureus- 5: 75 μM, S. typhimurium -8: 100 μM) treatments. Statistical significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test in ( e ) and ( f ). Data in panels c and d are representative of two biologically independent experiments. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Fig. 5 Anti-infectious efficacy of bacNIDs in S. aureus -infected skin wound. a Schematic illustrating the in vivo treatment timeline. b Representative images of the wound healing process in mice treated with PBS, GNPs, M-GNPs, S-GNPs, or bacNIDs. Scale bar, 1 cm. c In vivo wound closure rates in mice treated with PBS, GNPs, M-GNPs, S-GNPs, or bacNIDs at different time points. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 5 mice per group). d Immunohistochemical staining of IL-6 and TNF-α in mouse skin wound sections on day 7 after injury. Scale bar, 20 μm. e Quantitative histopathological analysis of IL-6 and TNF-α in PBS-, GNP-, M-GNP-, S-GNP-, or bacNID-treated skin wounds. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 mice per group). f Immunoblot data for CD31 and VEGF in skin wound under indicated treatments. g Immunohistochemical staining of CD31 and VEGF in mouse skin wound sections on day 7 after injury. Scale bar, 20 μm. h Quantitative histopathological analysis of CD31 and VEGF in PBS-, GNP-, M-GNP-, S-GNP-, or bacNID-treated wounds. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 3 mice per group). Statistical significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test in ( c , e ) and ( h ). Data in panels d and g are representative of three biologically independent experiments. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Fig. 7 Anti-infectious properties of bacNIDs against S . aureus -infected nonhealing keratitis model. a Schematic illustration of the nonhealing keratitis and in vivo treatment timeline. b Representative slit-lamp photomicrograph appearance of S. aureus -infected nonhealing keratitis on db/db mice. c Clinical score assessment (0 to 12) using three criteria (opacity area, surface regularity and opacity density) in mice with the indicated treatment. Data were presented as mean ± s.d. ( n = 5 mice per group). d H&E and MT staining of mice cornea section with indicated treatments on day 20 after injury. Scale bar, 100 μm. Data are representative of three biologically independent experiments. Statistical significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test in ( c ).
